items.title: Songs of Freedom Benefit Show For Women & Children of Ukraine to Feature Paul McCartney, Barbra Streisand, Sean Penn & More
items.summary:
A huge benefit show aimed at raising money for the women and children of Ukraine nearly five years into the country’s war against aggressor Russia will take place at Co-Op Live in Manchester, U.K. on Feb. 3, 2027.

According to the list of the first wave of announced performers, Songs of Freedom will feature sets from Bob Geldof, The Doobie Brothers, the Pretenders’ singer Chrissie Hynde, as well as the Lathums, Nick Lowe, Inspiral Carpets, Lottery Winners, Brooke Combe, Chris Difford, Midge Ure, Alabama 3, Graham Parker and Johnny & the Hardiwckes.

While a headliner act has not yet been revealed, the show is also slated to feature video appearances from Sir Paul McCartney, Barbra Streisand, Sean Penn, Ukrainian rockers Okean Elzy, Huey Lewis & the News, Ron Sexsmith, and Flyte.

“I am really pleased to have the opportunity to play my part in helping the Children and Communities in Ukraine,” said Live Aid producer Harvey Goldsmith in a statement. “This war has gone on far too long, and more and more children are suffering as a result. The concert at Co-Op in Manchester will highlight their plight. We must stand together and play a role in pressuring the need to stop this war.”

Proceeds from tickets sales will go to support a variety of organizations, including UNITED24 , Voices of Children , People of the Future and the Masha Foundation .

items.title: Taylor Swift returns to country roots for first CMA Awards performance in 13 Years with ‘Our Song’ and ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’
items.summary:
Taylor Swift returned to her country roots last night (Wednesday November 18) when she performed at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years.

READ MORE: Taylor Swift – ‘The Life Of A Showgirl’ review: magical when the songwriter just lets herself be 

The performance marked the pop star’s first appearance at the awards since 2016, when she presented Garth Brooks with the Entertainer of the Year award. It also marked her first time performing on the CMAs stage since 2013, when she performed ‘Red’ with Vince Gill and Alison Krauss .

For last night’s performance, Swift sported some bejewelled cowboy boots and broke out her track ‘ I Knew It, I Knew You ’, which was written for the Toy Story 5 soundtrack. She began the set backstage and moved through the hallways – passing by country stars including Lainey Wilson , Eric Church, Brad Paisley and more – as she made her way to the stage.

There, she threw things back to her early material by breaking out ‘Our Song’ from her 2006 self-titled debut album, and was joined by Keith Urban. Swift previously opened for the country legend during the early days of her career before she brought him out as a surprise guest on her ‘ 1989 World Tour ’ in 2015.

Urban also provided backing vocals for ‘That’s When’ and ‘We Were Happy’ on two ‘From The Vault’ tracks from ‘ Fearless (Taylor’s Version) ’, as well as covering her song ‘Lover’ on his 2019 tour. 

Swift first attended the CMA Awards when she released her debut solo album in 2006, and went on to win the Horizon Award – celebrating significant growth – the following year.

items.title: P!nk Adds 2028 Dates to Sphere Residency Due to Huge Demand: ‘This Is Crazy’
items.summary:
P!nk added another six-pack of dates to her residency run at Sphere in Las Vegas on Wednesday (Nov. 18). In an Instagram post announcing the 2028 shows, the “Trustfall” singer said she was blown away by the intense thirst for tickets to the first headlining shows by a solo female pop artist at the high-tech, multi-sensory venue.

“OK, this is crazy,” says P!nk in an accompanying video in which she hides her mouth under a blanket while chilling on a couch. “I’m nauseous! There’s three million people in line, on line … in line? On line? for the Sphere. I don’t know what to say. I think that’s the most people in the whole world and I’m gonna throw up … And … AHHHHHH!!!! We’re gonna add more shows.”

And so that’s what she did, tacking on a handful of 2028 shows on Jan. 19, 21, 22, 26, 28 and 29. The fresh run will also be accompanied by a trio of newly announced gigs on Nov. 3, 5 and 6, 2027.

P!nk, who is no stranger to high-wire acts, posted a video earlier this week of her trip to the top of the Sphere to shoot some promo shots in not ideal circumstances. “I’m not a weatherman, but I was right about the wind,” the singer said in the caption to a post featuring footage of the early morning shoot buffeted by 44 m.p.h. winds and sub 50-degree temperatures. “Coldest, scariest, most fun morning of my life. I LOVED IT!!!” the thrill-seeking pop star enthused. 

It will be P!nk’s first residency and she will make history as the first solo female pop star to join the long list of headliners Sphere has hosted to date, including: U2, Phish, Dead & Company, Anyma, Kenny Chesney,…
items.t: P!nk Adds 2028 Dates to Sphere Residency Due to Huge Demand: ‘This Is Crazy’

items.title: Trance, prog synths, guttural screaming: Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages is the year’s wildest electronic album
items.summary:
(Warp)
The Milan producer revisits his youth as a straight-edge punk fan voyeuristically dabbling in rave – and finds a thrilling interzone between both genres

The opening line of the biography on Lorenzo Senni’s Bandcamp page is striking. “Lorenzo Senni was never a raver,” it reads, something of a blunt admission from a dance producer, or at least a producer who works in an area of electronica influenced by dance music: one might reasonably assume you need some first-hand experience of the dancefloor’s ineffable freedom in order to make music for it. But the Milan-based Senni has made a USP out of his arm’s length distance from what that Bandcamp bio calls a “neon-hued chemical world”.

A straight-edge punk fan in the late 90s, he accompanied friends to Rimini’s hardcore and gabber clubs as a kind of anthropological exercise, a self-styled “rave voyeur” who “just liked to observe and analyse my surroundings”. Accordingly, his albums to date have dealt in what approving critics like to call deconstructions or interrogations of dance music rather than dance music itself: 2012’s Quantum Jelly and 2014’s Superimpositions featured what Senni called “pointillistic trance”, spinning the icy, staccato notes and arpeggiated synth lines of the genre’s epic breakdowns into lengthy, beatless tracks that never reached the climax implied. items.title: Beabadoobee live in London: Four albums in, she’s reached arena headline status her own way
items.summary:
Since releasing the alt-leaning slacker sensibilities of debut album ‘Fake It Flowers’ just as twee Powfu team-up ‘Death Bed (Coffee For Your Head)’ was sending her into the Top 10 of the UK singles chart, Beabadoobee has been hard to fully pin down. In her recent career, she’s played alongside the biggest pop spectacular on the planet as part of Taylor Swift ’s Eras Tour but also enlisted some of modern rock’s most celebrated names ( Hayley Williams , Turnstile ’s Brendan Yates, Deftones ’ Chino Moreno) on her latest LP ‘Pylon’ . Finally reaching the hallowed ground of an arena headliner in support of that fourth record, it’s a good time for Bea Laus to be tying all these sides together.

READ MORE:  Beabadoobee – ‘Pylon’ review: making peace with the mess of being in your mid-twenties 

“I remember playing here when I was 18 supporting The 1975 , and I couldn’t even imagine this would be on my cards,” she gushes in the encore before the whole crowd joins her in a singalong of whimsical acoustic number ‘The Way Things Go’. Where some of her peers have ascended to such levels within one album cycle, Beabadoobee’s journey has been slower. Tonight, playing with her band on a stage designed to look like an American freeway replete with dusty roadside foliage, a phone box pasted with ‘Missing’ signs bearing her likeness and a towering telephone pylon whose wires stretch and flicker out over the crowd, Laus has crafted an arena show that embraces her multiplicities. It’s not a pop gig or a rock gig, but a hybrid that satisfies both camps.

items.title: Tom Busby’s ‘Rockhampton Hangover’ Named 2026 Queensland Album of the Year
items.summary:
Tom Busby collects The Triffid’s 2026 Queensland Album of the Year with his debut solo longplay, Rockhampton Hangover .

The Rockhampton-raised singer and songwriter, Busby, one-half of the chart-topping blues and roots duo Busby Marou , beat out a shortlist of albums from the likes of Clea, Radium Dolls, Platonic Sex, 2 Charm and The Jungle Giants.

Now in its 11 th year, the public-voted award celebrates Queensland’s music community and was presented at Brisbane live music spot The Triffid, part of the Live Nation portfolio of venues.

Produced by Ben Kweller and recorded in the Texas Hill Country, the album is a meditation on family, home and finding your way through change.

“I’m pretty bloody stoked,” Busby says of his award. “It took me a long time to get around to making a solo record, and when I finally did, I kept coming back to stories from home. To have The Triffid name Rockhampton Hangover Album of the Year means a lot.  Big thanks to Ben Kweller for making it with me, to everyone who’s given it a spin and to The Triffid crew for backing Queensland music.”

“Tom has given so much to Queensland music through Busby Marou, so it’s great to see him take this step and have people really connect with the record,” adds John Collins, co-founder of The Triffid and bass player with Powderfinger , which is reuniting in 2027 for what promises to be one of the year’s biggest tours down under.

“Making your first solo album is a big thing,” he continues. “Having the fans vote it their favorite makes it even sweeter.”

items.title: CISAC’s International Standard Musical Work Codes System Hits 100 Million Songs Milestone
items.summary:
CISAC (the International Confederation of Societies of Authors and Composers) says its International Standard Musical Work Codes system — the tracking mechanism it created to identify and track individual songs — has hit the 100 million songs milestone.

“Behind every code is a song, a story, and the people who created it, CISAC’s director of business and technology said in a statement. “CISAC’s priority is to strengthen the connection between accurate data and fair remuneration for the creators the system serves.”

Related 

CISAC Reports Record Global Creator Royalties, Warns of ‘Largest Test’ From AI 

Rod Wave Indicted on Drug & Gun Charges for Items Allegedly Found in Car After Speeding Stop 

CL Signs With THEBLACKLABEL, Reuniting With Longtime Producer Teddy For 'Full Circle' Moment 

The first work assigned an ISWC code, or T-000.000.001.0, was ABBA’s “Dancing Queen” 30 years ago.

The code is an essential ingredient in ensuring songwriters get paid, especially in today’s world, where multiple collection societies around the globe track activity for each song, many of which have multiple songwriters. Each code provides a unique, permanent reference for a musical work, connecting it to information about its authors and composers, the announcement says, adding it has become key in sharing musical works data across the global network of song collection management organizations, also known as performance rights organizations in the U.S. Today, more than 100 societies around the globe are using the new system.

CISAC adds that close to 30 publishers are allocating ISWCs…
items.t: CISAC’s International Standard Musical Work Codes System Hits 100 Million Songs Milestone

items.title: 50 Cent Steps Out With Reebok G-Unit G6 Reboot
items.summary:
Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson ‘s reboot with Reebok is making a comeback, just in time for Christmas.

The hip-hop veteran recently teamed up with the sportswear specialist for the G-Unit G6, a blast from the past sneaker which were unveiled in August in its original red, white and blue colorway and proved to be a hit with 50 Cent’s followers. Those shoes re-launch globally on Friday, Nov. 20 .

The basketball and street fashion-inspired gear initially rolled out in 2003, the year when Fifty blew up on airwaves and charts around the globe. The one that got away, “In Da Club,” logged nine weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100, and the New Yorker followed it up two months later with “21 Questions,” featuring the late Nate Dogg, which spent a full month atop the national singles survey. His smash album Get Rich or Die Tryin’ held the top spot on the Billboard 200 for six weeks, and lent its name to the 2005 semi-autobiographical film, which gave 50 Cent his first starring role.

That partnership made Jackson one of the first musicians to lead a major footwear franchise. “Creating it the first time was special,” Jackson recounts in an interview with GQ . “I worked with Todd (Krinsky) and the team on everything and they really let me make it mine. It wasn’t just a sneaker—it became part of the culture.”

Krinsky, who started with Reebok in 1993, working in the mailroom, is now CEO. “Our relationship with 50 has always gone beyond sneakers,” he remarks in a statement. “He helped define an important chapter in Reebok’s history, and together we created something that had a lasting impact on…
items.t: 50 Cent Steps Out With Reebok G-Unit G6 Reboot

items.title: ‘Never Go Backwards, Just Make Things Bigger and Better’: How Paul O’Neill Chartered Trans-Siberian Orchestra’s Journey Ahead
items.summary:
When Trans-Siberian Orchestra turned 20 back in 2016, the troupe’s enduring success was as surprising to founder Paul O’Neill as anyone in or outside of the camp.

“I would love to say that we planned for it to resonate like this, but it was just pure luck,” acknowledged O’Neill, who passed away the following year at the age of 61 . And that it was an endeavor almost entirely based around the Christmas holiday made it seem even less likely.

“Normally you have five or six other platinum albums, then you take on Christmas,” O’Neill noted. “Of course, we took it on first and the rest of the year on later. It’s all worked out.”

That’s certainly an understatement for TSO, which celebrates the 30th anniversary of its triple-platinum debut album, Christmas Eve and Other Stories , this year with its annual, two-company concert tour opening Nov. 19 in Green Bay, Wisc., and Council Bluffs, Iowa. The 97 performances through Dec. 30 will again feature the soundtrack and narration from The Ghosts of Christmas Eve , TSO’s 1999 made-for-TV film, and other material amidst the usual fusillade of arena-filling special effects and pyrotechnics, with two shows a day at most stops.

During the past three decades TSO has released six studio albums — four platinum or better, three Christmas-themed — and an EP, along with the multi-platinum singles “Christmas Eve/Sarajevo 12/24” and “Christmas Cannon.” The 2005 track “Wizards in Winter” also hit platinum, and a fan’s synchronized home display soundtracked by the tune was turned into an ad campaign for Miller Lite.

items.title: 2026 CMA Awards Performances, Ranked
items.summary:
The night belonged to Ella Langley at Wednesday evening’s (Nov. 18) CMA Awards . Propelled by the success of “Choosin’ Texas,” her album Dandelion and a headlining tour, Langley won her first entertainer of the year honor. She also won female vocalist of the year, single, song and music video of the year (all for “Choosin’ Texas”) and picked up album of the year, for Dandelion .

“I have watched these awards since I was a little kid, and the award I cared most about was song of the year and entertainer of the year,” Langley said in accepting the CMA entertainer of the year honor, adding, “[there] hasn’t been a song on the radio or in my ears at all where I wasn’t imagining what that song would sound like in front of a crowd…”

Other winners during the night included Chris Stapleton, Stephen Wilson Jr., Brooks & Dunn, The Red Clay Strays and the song “McArthur,” from HARDY, Morgan Wallen, Eric Church and Tim McGraw. Lainey Wilson, hosting for a third time, opened the show by paying tribute to the late music legend Dolly Parton.

“Dolly gave us hope, Dolly gave us joy, Dolly gave us her heart,” Wilson said.

Wilson was joined at times to host by Luke Bryan, and also Brad Paisley, in a throwback to the decade-plus that Paisley and Carrie Underwood hosted the CMAs. From there, the evening celebrated the CMA Awards’ six decades of helping to showcase artists on one of country music’s biggest stages.

items.title: NØ MAN Will Stab You In The Eye
items.summary:
The first time I heard the word "Lynchburg," or at least the first time than I can remember hearing it, I thought it was a joke. In the opening scenes from Escape From LA , John Carpenter's slightly misbegotten 1996 sequel to his classic Escape From New York , a voiceover describes a bleak future in which the US elects a hardline Christian Nationalist president, who then declares himself dictator for life and moves the US capital to his Lynchburg hometown. The film never names that president, though he's played by Cliff Robertson, the square-jawed Oscar-winning actor and future Uncle Ben. When I saw that movie in the theater, I thought everything about this president was a wild exaggeration, including his decision to relocate federal operations to this surely made-up place that's basically called Racist Murderville.

items.title: Elena Pinderhughes’ Time Has Come
items.summary:
Flutist Elena Pinderhughes has been on the scene for over a decade. Many people likely first spotted her name when she appeared as a credited guest on “Sunrise In Beijing” and “Liberation Over Gangsterism,” two tracks from Chief Adjuah’s 2015 album Stretch Music . She was part of his band for the Centennial Trilogy ( Ruler Rebel , Diaspora , and The Emancipation Procrastination ), Ancestral Recall , and the live Axiom . She’s also worked with Ambrose Akinmusire, Terri Lyne Carrington, Immanuel Wilkins, Terrace Martin, Meshell Ndegeocello, Herbie Hancock, her brother Samora Pinderhughes, and more. But somehow she’s only releasing her debut album now.

items.title: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou
items.summary:
He was nearly an early rock’n’roll star but took a different path, from Fats Domino to the Band and pro-environment songwriting. As a career-spanning box set is released, those who knew him remember an American original

‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.”

Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange guy, a loner,” says one of his Louisiana contemporaries, 88-year-old Johnnie Allan. “He knew what he had and wouldn’t compromise.” Now a box set, The Bobby Charles Story, containing almost every recording Charles released, aims to establish the Cajun magus as one of the greats.

items.title: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?
items.summary:
The Scottish quartet existed for just three years at the turn of the millennium. But after Frank Ocean and TikTok thrilled to Sue Tompkins’ unique vocals, they’re back. They explain their fears about ‘spoiling the joy’

‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.”

On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers.”

items.title: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business
items.summary:
She threw a (metaphorical) brick through Spotify’s window and exposed industry failings with her ‘Butts for Tour Buses’ campaign. Now the singer is embracing her Irish roots with her new album’s fighting spirit

Kate Nash was standing on a fire truck in a showgirl outfit complete with white tights and pink G-string, shouting through a loudhailer about the music industry’s failure to pay artists fairly, when she wondered if she’d gone too far. It was 2024 and the truck, which made pit stops outside the London offices of Spotify and Live Nation, had a large black-and-white picture of Nash’s bum on the back along with the words “Butts for Tour Buses” – a reference to her newly launched OnlyFans account, which she was using to fund her tour.

That afternoon, she called her manager Kat. “I told her: ‘I’ve thrown a brick through the window at Spotify.’ She went: ‘What, literally?’ and I said: ‘No, but I’ve been standing outside their offices with a megaphone, so that relationship is over. I don’t think we’ll be making their New Music Friday feature.’ And we didn’t.” [see footnote]

items.title: Ocean Colour Scene review – no other band of their era can do it like this
items.summary:
Ulster Hall, Belfast
With two sets of fathers and sons now in the group, as they play all of Moseley Shoals on its 30th anniversary, the indie stalwarts have aged into seismic and soulful performers

‘It’s only 30 years ago,” Simon Fowler says of Moseley Shoals. He would seem to mean it, but 30 years makes Ocean Colour Scene’s breakthrough album as old now as Revolver was when they were making it. The band once derided for raiding the 60s are now heritage themselves. They open the album’s anniversary tour on the stage where Led Zeppelin first played Stairway to Heaven, and you can’t help but appreciate the lineage.

They walk on to Green Onions, fresh from the Crown Bar, and open with You’ve Got It Bad, all supreme Motown stomp. Fowler sings with a hand in his pocket and looks taken aback by the welcome. The casualness is a conduit: his voice has aged into something close to peak Joe Cocker, grained at the edges, honey underneath. Lining Your Pockets is more resounding than ever.

items.title: Paris Paloma review – arena-scale alt-pop drama from a singer on her way to bigger things
items.summary:
Bristol Beacon
The UK artist combines feminist fury with accessible melodies and a dramatic flair that sees her alternately pogoing and seeking out the wind machines at the prow of the stage

People are dancing to a song they don’t know, with flower garlands in their hair and their arms around their friends. This reaction to Fairy Dance, an unreleased track written about the community that has sprung up around her music, says a lot about the moment Paris Paloma finds herself in, and tonight’s show feels for all the world like a stepping stone to bigger things.

Throughout, Paloma leans in to the built-in drama of songs from her second album, The Fatal Flaw, which pairs ornate folk arrangements with the sort of arena-sized alt-pop production favoured by Florence + the Machine. With a sculpture inspired by surrealist Ithell Colquhoun’s Tree of Veins dominating the stage, she falls to her knees to deliver high notes and seeks out wind machines at the prow of the stage, her flowing crimson dress buffeted as if on a wintry moor.
